ai.literal: Like the earth that bears those who dig it, bearing those who insult them is the foremost virtue.
ai.translation: Just as the earth supports those who dig into it, bearing with those who insult us is the foremost virtue.
ai.modern: தன்னைத் தோண்டுபவர்களைத் தாங்கி நிற்கும் பூமியைப் போல, தம்மை இகழ்ந்து பேசுபவர்களைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்வது மிகச் சிறந்த பண்பாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet introduces the chapter on forbearance using a powerful simile. The earth does not collapse or strike back when people dig into it; instead, it patiently supports them. Similarly, when others insult or despise us, the best response is to bear with them patiently. This quality of patience is hailed here as the foremost of all virtues.

ai.literal: Forbearing transgression always, that forgetting than-that is-better.
ai.translation: To always forgive an injury is good; to forget it is even better than that.
ai.modern: பிறர் செய்யும் வரம்பு மீறிய தீங்கைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்வது எப்போதும் நல்லது; அத்தீங்கினை மனதிலிருந்து மறந்துவிடுவது அதைக் காட்டிலும் மிகவும் நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet outlines a hierarchy of virtues when dealing with wrongs committed by others. The word 'iṟappu' refers to a transgression, excess, or injury that crosses acceptable boundaries. While 'poṟuttal' (forbearing or enduring) such an act is always a noble and necessary practice, the poet asserts that 'maṟatthal' (forgetting) the incident entirely is even better ('naṉṟu'). Forgetting ensures that no trace of resentment or bitterness remains in the mind, elevating the act of forgiveness to its highest state.

ai.literal: Poverty within poverty is turning away a guest; strength within strength is bearing with the foolish.
ai.translation: The worst of poverty is turning away a guest; the greatest of strength is bearing with the foolish.
ai.modern: வறுமையிலும் கொடிய வறுமை வீட்டிற்கு வந்த விருந்தினரைத் தவிர்ப்பது ஆகும்; வலிமையிலும் சிறந்த வலிமை அறிவற்றவர்களின் தீமைகளைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்வது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two extremes to highlight the supreme value of patience. It states that the ultimate form of poverty is not the lack of material wealth, but the inability to welcome and feed a guest. Conversely, the ultimate form of strength is not physical power, but the mental fortitude required to patiently endure the actions of ignorant or foolish people. Through this comparison, the poet elevates forbearance to the highest virtue of the strong.

ai.literal: Fullness of character not departing if one desires, possession of forbearance cherishing to practice is fit.
ai.translation: If one desires that fullness of character never departs from them, they must cherish and practice forbearance.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் தன்னிடம் உள்ள நிறைவான நற்பண்புகள் நீங்காமல் இருக்க விரும்பினால், அவர் பொறுமையைப் போற்றிப் பின்பற்ற வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the relationship between self-control or moral completeness (நிறையுடைமை) and forbearance (பொறையுடைமை). The author states that if a person wishes to retain their noble qualities and integrity without losing them, they must actively cherish and practice patience. Here, 'நிறை' refers to the abundance of good virtues and self-discipline, while 'பொறை' represents the capacity to endure wrongs. Thus, forbearance is presented as the essential protective shield that preserves all other virtues from slipping away.

ai.literal: Those who retaliated, as a thing of worth they will not esteem; they will treasure those who forbore, wrapping them up like gold.
ai.translation: The wise will not esteem those who retaliate as worthy of any notice; but they will treasure those who patiently endure, wrapping them up like precious gold.
ai.modern: தீமை செய்தவரைத் தண்டித்தவர்களை ஒரு பொருட்டாக மதிக்க மாட்டார்கள்; ஆனால், அத்தீமையைப் பொறுத்துக் கொண்டவர்களைப் பொன்னைப் போலப் போற்றி மனத்தில் வைப்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts how the world remembers those who take revenge versus those who practice forgiveness. The poet uses 'ஒறுத்தாரை' to denote those who retaliate, stating that they are not esteemed as anything of worth ('ஒன்றாக வையாரே'). In contrast, those who show forbearance ('பொறுத்தாரை') are highly valued. They are compared to 'பொன்' (gold), which is carefully wrapped ('பொதிந்து') and preserved as a treasure. True honor and lasting remembrance belong not to the vengeful, but to those who patiently endure wrongs.

ai.literal: To those who punish, one day's pleasure; to those who endure, fame until the very end.
ai.translation: For those who retaliate, the pleasure lasts but for a single day; for those who patiently endure, their fame will last until the end of time.
ai.modern: தவறு செய்தவர்களைத் தண்டித்தவருக்கு ஒரு நாள் மட்டுமே இன்பம் கிடைக்கும்; ஆனால் பொறுத்துக் கொண்டவருக்கு உலகம் அழியும் வரை புகழ் நிலைத்து நிற்கும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts the fleeting satisfaction of taking revenge with the everlasting glory of patience and forgiveness. Those who punish or retaliate against wrongdoers experience a momentary, single day's pleasure of satisfaction. In contrast, those who choose to patiently endure and forgive earn a lasting reputation and fame that endures until the very end of time. The word 'பொன்றும்' refers to perishing or ending, and 'துணையும்' acts as a limit, indicating that their fame will remain as long as the world itself exists.

ai.literal: Even if others do improper things to oneself, feeling pain and not doing unvirtuous things is good.
ai.translation: Even if others do improper and harmful things to you, it is best to feel pity for the pain they might suffer and refrain from doing anything unvirtuous in return.
ai.modern: தமக்குத் தகுதியில்லாத தீமைகளைப் பிறர் செய்தாலும், அதனால் வரும் துன்பத்திற்கு வருந்தி, அறமல்லாத செயல்களை அவர்களுக்குச் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே நல்லது.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the peak of patience and forbearance. When others do improper or harmful things (tiṟaṉalla) to us, our natural reaction might be revenge. However, the poet advises us to feel pity or sorrow (nō nōntu) for the pain or consequences that the wrongdoer might face, and to absolutely refrain from returning unvirtuous deeds (aṟaṉalla ceyyāmai). By choosing not to retaliate, we preserve our own virtue and demonstrate true strength of character.

ai.literal: Those who did harmful deeds by arrogance, oneself, by one's own forbearance, having conquered, should conquer completely.
ai.translation: Conquer with your own forbearance those who, out of arrogance, have done harmful deeds to you.
ai.modern: செருக்கினால் தீமைகளைச் செய்தவர்களை, நாம் நம்முடைய பொறுமையால் வென்றுவிட வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the ultimate way to respond to insolence and harm. When people commit wrongful acts against us out of arrogance (மிகுதி), our natural instinct might be to retaliate. However, the poet advises us to conquer them using our own forbearance and dignified conduct (தகுதி). By remaining patient and righteous, we disarm their hostility and achieve a true, noble victory over their bad behavior.

ai.literal: Than those who have renounced, purity possess they who endure harsh words from the mouth of those who have transgressed limits.
ai.translation: Those who endure harsh words from the mouths of people who transgress all bounds of decency possess a purity greater than even those who have renounced the world.
ai.modern: வரம்பு மீறி நடப்பவர்களுடைய வாயிலிருந்து வரும் துன்பம் தரும் சொற்களைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்பவர்கள், உலகத்தைத் துறந்தவர்களை விடவும் மேலான தூய்மை உடையவர்கள் ஆவர்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares the spiritual purity of those who practice patience with that of ascetics who have renounced the world. The word 'இறந்தார்' refers to those who have crossed the boundaries of proper conduct and decency. When such people utter 'இன்னாச்சொல்' (painful or abusive words), the act of enduring them ('நோற்கிற்பவர்') requires immense self-control. The poet asserts that this quiet endurance represents a higher level of moral and spiritual purity ('தூய்மை') than the formal renunciation ('துறந்தார்') of worldly life. Thus, patience is elevated to the highest form of spiritual practice.

ai.literal: Those who perform penance without eating are great; (but they are) behind those who endure the harsh words spoken by others.
ai.translation: Those who perform penance by fasting are indeed great, but they stand only behind those who patiently endure the harsh words spoken by others.
ai.modern: உணவு உண்ணாமல் நோன்பு நோற்பவர்கள் பெருமை உடையவர்கள் ஆவர்; ஆனால், அவர்கள் பிறர் பேசும் கொடுமையான சொற்களைப் பொறுத்துக் கொள்பவர்களுக்குப் பின்னேதான் நிற்பார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares physical fasting with emotional forbearance. While fasting (abstaining from food) is traditionally considered a high spiritual achievement, the poet argues that enduring the bitter, hurtful words of others requires a far greater strength of character. Therefore, those who practice patience and forgiveness are placed on a higher pedestal than those who merely subject their bodies to physical austerities. The key word 'நோல்' (to endure or perform penance) is used in both contexts to show that bearing insults is itself the ultimate form of penance.
